claims.text: Controlled silicon doping of the near-surface region can promote formation of a Si-rich interfacial layer on boride-based components.
The proposed Si-rich interfacial layer is likely to contain silicide phases.
The Si-rich interfacial layer can act as a diffusion barrier.
Formation of the Si-rich barrier would improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Laser surface alloying can be used to introduce a modest silicon concentration into the near-surface region.
Temperatures of approximately 700–800 °C are typical of the relevant hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure.
During high-temperature exposure, added silicon reacts with the boride surface to form a silicide phase.
The resulting silicide phase is stable during molten-aluminum exposure.
The resulting silicide phase is self-healing.
The silicide phase retards direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The silicide phase retards diffusion of molten-aluminum species into the component.
Retarding contact and diffusion reduces molten-aluminum corrosion attack.
Silicon-doped surfaces will exhibit lower corrosion penetration than untreated boride-based components under identical exposure conditions.
Silicon-doped surfaces will exhibit less weight loss than untreated boride-based components under identical exposure conditions.
Too little near-surface silicon may be ineffective.
Excessive near-surface silicon may produce brittle phases.
The protective effect is expected specifically under high-temperature hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions and may not extend to substantially different environments.
